content.text:
Lighthouses are among the oldest engineered structures people have built for a purpose that remains the same: to tell a sailor where land is. Their history is in part a history of fire, of the fuels and lamps that carried it, and of the optics that eventually made a small flame visible for dozens of miles. It is also a history of stone and mortar set against the sea, and of the administrative bodies that paid for them, lit them, and eventually switched them off.

The most famous early example was the Pharos of Alexandria, built on the small island of Pharos at the entrance to the harbour of the Egyptian city. Construction is usually dated to the reign of Ptolemy II in the early third century BC, and the architect is traditionally given as Sostratus of Cnidus, though the ancient sources that name him are not contemporary. The tower was a massive limestone structure, perhaps between one hundred and one hundred and thirty metres high by most estimates, with a square base, an octagonal middle section, and a cylindrical top. A fire burned at its summit, probably fed by wood or oil, and some ancient writers claimed that a polished metal mirror reflected the light outward, though no surviving description confirms the mechanism. The Pharos became so admired that its name entered several languages as the word for a beacon, and it was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Earthquakes weakened it over the centuries, and by the fourteenth century its remains had collapsed. Some of its stones were reportedly reused in the fortress that the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built on the same site.

The Roman world built many lighthouses of its own, and some survive in altered form. The Tower of Hercules at A Coruña, on the northwest coast of Spain, dates to the late first or early second century AD and is the oldest lighthouse still in operation. Its core is a square Roman masonry tower, faced and extended in later centuries, and it still guides ships into a rocky coast. The Romans used lighthouses to mark harbours and dangerous approaches along the Mediterranean and the Atlantic coasts of their provinces, and the surviving examples show a standard method: a tall masonry shaft, a fire at the top, and a stone or brick structure built to withstand both weather and the occasional attack.

After the fall of Rome in the west, the lighthouse tradition thinned out in Europe, though it never disappeared. Coastal communities kept fires burning on headlands and church towers, and religious houses sometimes maintained beacons for pilgrims and merchants. In the Middle Ages, lights were often a local responsibility, supported by tolls, dues on shipping, or the piety of a guild or monastery. Hook Head, on the south coast of Ireland, has a claim to be the oldest operating lighthouse in the English-speaking world, with a tower whose origins go back to the twelfth century, though it has been rebuilt and modernised many times since. In Italy, the Lanterna of Genoa, first recorded in the twelfth century, became a symbol of the city and was rebuilt more than once after damage and fire.

Early modern lighthouses were mostly coal fires. A coal brazier burned in an open iron basket at the top of a tower, and a keeper had to tend it through the night, feed it, and clear the ash. Coal was heavy, smoky, and expensive to carry to remote rocks, and the fire gave a light that was weak, unevenly bright, and easy to confuse with other lights along the same coast. The brazier was also dangerous, since a stray spark could set fire to the lantern room or the wooden fittings that often surrounded it.

The most important early modern development was not in the flame but in the structure beneath it. Rocky reefs far from shore were the places where ships were most often lost, and building on them was difficult. The first Eddystone lighthouse, off Plymouth in England, was a timber structure begun by Henry Winstanley in 1696. It was a fanciful building, decorated with ornamental work, and it lasted only until the great storm of November 1703, when it was swept away with Winstanley himself inside. A second lighthouse, designed by John Rudyerd and built with a more sensible profile of wood and stone, served from 1709 until a fire destroyed it in 1755.

The third Eddystone was the work of John Smeaton, an engineer who had a scientific temperament and a habit of testing materials. Smeaton studied hydraulic lime, a cement that would set under water, and he used the stone and mortar in a new way: the courses of granite were dovetailed and locked together, each block shaped to fit its neighbours, so that the tower behaved more like a single monolith than a stack of separate stones. The lighthouse was completed in 1759 and stood until the rock beneath it was undermined in the late nineteenth century. Its upper part was then taken down and re-erected on Plymouth Hoe, where it still stands as a monument. Smeaton's principles of interlocking masonry and carefully tested lime shaped the designs of many later sea towers, and his work is often treated as the founding moment of modern marine engineering.

The problem of the light itself was addressed in the late eighteenth century. In the 1780s, the Swiss chemist Aimé Argand developed a lamp with a tubular wick and a glass chimney that created a draught, producing a flame that burned brighter and more steadily than a candle or an ordinary oil lamp. Reflectors of polished metal or silvered glass were placed behind the lamps to throw the light outward, and the combination of lamp and reflector was an important step forward. Still, the reflectors had their limits, because they could not capture much of the light that spread in directions away from the observer.

The decisive advance came from the French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel. Working in the 1810s, Fresnel designed a lens built from concentric rings of glass prisms, each ring bending light so that it emerged as a nearly parallel beam. His lens captured far more of the lamp's output than any reflector, and it could be arranged in tiers to form a tall, nearly cylindrical apparatus around the flame. Fresnel's first lenses were installed at the Cordouan lighthouse at the mouth of the Gironde in 1823, and within a few decades such lenses were in use across Europe and in the American colonies and later the United States. The French lighthouse service, and its counterparts elsewhere, adopted the principle of the optic as a standard, and the different lenses were given characteristic arrangements of flashes and eclipses so that a mariner could identify a particular light by its pattern.

The nineteenth century brought a surge of construction, financed by governments, trinity houses, and maritime boards. In Britain, the Trinity House corporation, which had held a royal charter since the sixteenth century, managed a growing network of lights, and engineers such as Robert Stevenson built rock towers far out at sea, including the Bell Rock light off the Scottish coast, completed in 1810 after years of hard work in a tidal reef. Stevenson's family would go on to build a long line of lighthouses around the Scottish coast, and the family's engineering standards became a model. In the United States, the Lighthouse Board, established in 1852, took over the administration of the nation's lights, which had previously been managed in a patchwork of local arrangements. The board standardised equipment, built new towers, and set the pattern for a federal service that would last for more than a century.

Lighthouse keeping was a demanding life. Keepers and their families often lived on remote rocks or islands, cut off from land for weeks at a time by weather. They trimmed wicks, polished lenses, wound clockwork mechanisms that turned the optic, recorded the weather, and sometimes rowed out to rescue shipwrecked sailors. Their logs survive in archives on both sides of the Atlantic and form a valuable record of the work. Many keepers were men with families who depended on a small and uncertain wage. In some services, women served as keepers, and in others the families of keepers took up many of the daily tasks.

The twentieth century changed the trade through technology. Paraffin and then electricity replaced oil and coal as fuels, and vaporised oil and gas lamps spread to outlying lights. Electric lamps, automatic timers, and sealed mechanisms reduced the need for constant human attention. Radio beacons and, later, satellite navigation took over much of the lighthouse's navigational role for large ships, though lights remained important as visual marks and as backups. Through the later decades of the century, most lighthouses in the developed world were automated, and the keepers were withdrawn. Many towers were sold, handed to trusts, or converted into museums, hostels, and private homes, and some of the most remote lights were left to run on solar power and batteries with occasional maintenance visits.

The lighthouse has thus gone through a long arc, from an ancient fire on a harbour island, to Roman masonry on a rocky coast, to the carefully engineered granite of the Eddystone and the glass rings of Fresnel's lens, to the solar-powered automatic lights of the present. The purpose has barely changed in more than two thousand years. What has changed is the means by which a light could be made to reach further, burn more reliably, and tell a sailor exactly where he stood, and the people who built, tended, and eventually stopped tending these towers have left a record that still shapes the coast they once guarded.
